title: The year of delegations
hook: tribes from all over Arabia come to Medina

segments.voice: Yesterday, sidq, and Ka'b, who could have talked his way out and said instead: I had no excuse. Your line was the truth saved them.

Bags in the hallway, someone always at the door, the kettle never cold. That's a house with guests for a week. Medina had a whole season of it. After Mecca opened and the army came back from Tabuk, the tribes of Arabia started arriving: from Yemen in the south, from the Gulf coast in the east, from the desert tribes and the mountain towns. Poets, chiefs, farmers, men who'd fought against him a year before. Muslim historians gave that stretch of time a name: wufud.
screen: `A HOUSE FULL OF GUESTS.` → `FROM YEMEN, THE GULF, THE DESERT.` → `THE YEAR OF DELEGATIONS.`

segments.voice: Some delegations came to accept Islam. Some came to make a treaty. Some came to look him over and argue. The Qur'an even records one group that stood outside his private rooms and shouted for him to come out, and it says gently that it would have been better if they had waited. That season, the Prophet ﷺ spent much of his time receiving them, and the reports say he received them well: he gave them a place to stay, fed them, and gave gifts when they left. One visit the biographers tell at length came from Najran, in the south: a delegation of Christians who came to talk about Jesus, long and hard. The early biographer Ibn Ishaq reports that when their time of prayer came, they prayed in the Prophet's mosque, and when some people moved to stop them, he said, let them. They went home with a treaty that protected their churches. Scholars discuss how strong that report is, but it's told and retold. A short surah that commentators connect with this season says, in Pickthall's words: "thou seest mankind entering the religion of Allah in troops." And what does it tell him to do at that moment of success? Praise his Lord, and ask forgiveness. Not a victory lap. Even at the very end, the hadith say, lying ill, one of his last instructions was to keep giving gifts to delegations the way he had. The door stayed open to the end.
screen: `TO ACCEPT, TO TREAT, TO ARGUE.` · `FED, HOUSED, GIVEN GIFTS.` · `THE CHRISTIANS OF NAJRAN.` · `ENTERING IN TROOPS.` · then, large: `THEY CAME FROM EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Think of the next person who'll come to your door, your desk or your table: a neighbor, a new coworker, a friend of a friend, a delivery driver. Picture them arriving, and yourself stopping what you're doing, looking up, and offering one small gift: a glass of water, a real question, their name said warmly. If you pray, you can ask for an open door.
Wufud, delegations: tribes from every corner of Arabia came to Medina that year, and found the door open.
Your line: they came from everywhere. Friends, old enemies and strangers alike. Day two hundred eighty-three, done.

howItsDone: Muslims honor guests as part of the sunnah, offering food, a place to rest and gifts, and surah an-Nasr (110), on people entering the religion in troops, is often taught alongside the story of this season.
